study.title: 2 Corinthians 6 - Faithful ministry, open heart and separation to God
study.overview: In this chapter, Paul shows that the grace received cannot be treated as something empty: it requires immediate response, obedient faith and consistent life. He recalls that the time of salvation is now and describes, with concrete examples, how true ministry endures afflictions without losing purity, patience and love. Then he opens his heart to the Corinthians, appealing to an affective and spiritual reconciliation. The chapter ends with a strong exhortation that the people of God do not unite closely with unbelievers in order to compromise their identity, for believers are a temple of the living God and called to live in holy separation, sustained by the promise of divine adoption.

outline.title: The grace received should not be wasted
outline.explanation: Paul asks that the Corinthians not to receive in vain the grace of God and show that the prophetic promise of salvation is already in force: the favorable time is now. The correct answer to the gospel is to welcome you with faith and reconciliation.

outline.title: The Character of God Approved Ministry
outline.explanation: The apostle describes his service not to put an impediment before the gospel. He enumerates sufferings, trials and paradoxes of ministerial life, but also spiritual virtues and firmness, showing that the work of God advances without relying on human appearance.

outline.title: The opening of the apostolic heart
outline.explanation: Paul speaks with tenderness to the Corinthians. He claims that they have not lacked love or space in their hearts, and asks, as one who speaks to children, to respond with the same expansion of affection and communion.

outline.title: Don't hold on to bonds that contradict holiness
outline.explanation: Paul forbids intimate union with unbelievers in terms of spiritual partnership, contrasting justice and injustice, light and darkness, Christ and evil. The foundation is the identity of believers as a temple of God, called separation and purity, with the promise that God will receive them as sons and daughters.

study.context: The chapter continues Paul's appeal for reconciliation with the church of Corinth, after his previous exhortations on the ministry of reconciliation. The notes highlight that he writes to win the Corinthians back to the truth of the gospel and to fellowship with him. The text also uses language of the Old Testament: the promise of acceptable time comes from Isaiah, and the promise of sonship comes from 2 Samuel, with additional echo of Isaiah in the mention of sons and daughters. On the final section, the notes record that some scholars understand 14-7:1 as an inserted excerpt from another letter, while others see it as a legitimate digression of Paul; this question remains discussed.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter unites grace, human response, and sanctification. The grace of God is offered in a real and urgent way; therefore, rejecting or burning it is grave. The authentic Christian ministry is not measured by comfort, but by fidelity in the midst of afflictions, preserving purity, knowledge, patience, kindness, and the action of the Holy Spirit. Paul also shows that the church is not only a religious group, but the temple of the living God; this requires separation from covenants that compromise loyalty to Christ. The identity of believers culminates in the promise of adoption: God treats them as sons and daughters, which reveals both intimacy and holy belonging. Holiness, therefore, is not proud isolation, but fidelity to the God who dwells in the midst of his people.

scholarViews.insight: Isaiah's quotation reinforces that the offer of salvation is decisive and that reconciliation with God must produce reconciliation between Paul and the Corinthians.
Paul speaks with great tenderness in opening the heart to the Corinthians and treating them as children, preparing the exhortation to communion and the removal of evil.
Paul promises that God will be the Father of believers and that they will be his sons and daughters, highlighting the language of family and the security of the relationship with the Almighty Lord.

questions: In which areas can I be receiving God's grace superficially, without a practical answer of faith and obedience?
What partnerships, habits or influences can be weakening my allegiance to Christ and my holiness?
My way of treating other believers reveals an open and reconciling heart, like Paul's?
study.practice: This week, examine a relationship, commitment, or influence that is shaping your spiritual choices. If it contradicts her fidelity to Christ, establish clear limits and guide herself through prayer, Scripture, and godly counsel. At the same time, practice the opening of the heart: try to reconcile with someone, to speak with truth and to act with purity, patience and goodness, remembering that you belong to the living God and is called to live as your son or daughter.
study.uncertainty: The note on 6:14-7:1 records a real academic discussion: some see this excerpt as the insertion of another letter, while others understand it as Paul's tour. In addition, although the notes associate the expression 'air emission' or 'enlarged heart' the affective language, the exact detailing of the metaphor should be treated with caution. There is no firm data in the notes about dates, geography or broader historical context beyond what is explicitly mentioned.
